findings.title: Strategy close shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, so messages after a rebalance are dropped and committed
findings.description:
The pool is created once in the factory `__init__` (`result_consumer.py:133`) and the same instance is handed to every strategy built by `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` (`result_consumer.py:254-259`). But `close()`, `terminate()` and `join()` on the strategy all call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which stops the workers and shuts down every queue (`queue_consumer.py:231-243`). Nothing restarts them.

Arroyo closes and joins the strategy on partition revocation, then calls `create_with_partitions` again on assignment. For the new strategy:
- `FixedQueuePool.submit` registers the offset and then `work_queue.put` raises `queue.ShutDown` (`queue_consumer.py:211-212`).
- `queue.ShutDown` is an `Exception`, so the blanket handler in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` logs it and marks the offset complete (`queue_consumer.py:317-325`).
- The commit loop then commits that offset.

The result is permanent, silent data loss for the rest of the process lifetime. The shared `OffsetTracker` also carries `last_committed` and `outstanding` state for revoked partitions into the next assignment.

Fix: give the pool a single owner. Either the factory owns it and the strategy only stops its commit thread and drains, or each strategy creates its own pool and tracker. No test calls `create_with_partitions` twice, which is why this is not caught.

findings.title: Blanket `except Exception` in `submit` turns any enqueue failure into a committed, unprocessed message
findings.description: Any failure in decoding, grouping or enqueueing is logged and the offset is marked complete. That is reasonable for a poison payload, but it also covers infrastructure failures such as a shut-down queue, and it is what makes the finding above silent. Limit the skip-and-commit path to decode failures and let the rest propagate so the consumer crashes instead of committing past unprocessed data.

findings.title: Queues are unbounded, contradicting the documented backpressure guarantee
findings.description: The class docstring promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up" (`queue_consumer.py:253`), but each queue is `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises `MessageRejected`. If workers are slower than ingest, or one hot subscription stalls a queue, the consumer keeps reading and memory grows without limit, both in the queues and in the tracker's offset sets. Each `WorkItem` also holds the full original `message`, which is never read (`queue_consumer.py:31`). Use bounded queues and raise `MessageRejected` when full, and drop the unused field.

findings.title: Committable-offset calculation requires contiguous offsets and stalls forever on a gap
findings.description: `get_committable_offsets` walks `range(start, max_offset + 1)` and stops at the first offset not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed contiguous (compaction, transaction markers). A single gap means that partition never commits again and `all_offsets` grows unbounded. Because one thread submits each partition in offset order, the contiguity check adds no safety: "highest seen offset below the smallest outstanding one" is sufficient and gap-tolerant. The tests lock in the gap-blocking behaviour (`test_offset_gaps_block_commits`, `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps`).

findings.title: Shutdown is not graceful and `join` ignores its timeout
findings.description:
- **No drain:** `shutdown()` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before `q.shutdown(immediate=False)`, so each worker exits after its current item (`queue_consumer.py:129`) and queued items are abandoned despite the "Gracefully" docstring.
- **Late completions uncommitted:** `close()` joins the commit thread before stopping the pool (`queue_consumer.py:336-338`), so anything finishing during shutdown is not committed and will be reprocessed.
- **Timeout ignored:** `join(timeout)` discards its argument (`queue_consumer.py:344-345`); the worst case is 5s for the commit thread plus 5s per worker, joined sequentially.
- **Unverified:** the final commit is called without `force=True`, so arroyo's commit policy may throttle it, and `commit` is invoked from a background thread. I could not confirm either behaviour against arroyo's source.

findings.title: Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and passes only by timing
findings.description: `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` says errors "don't block offset commits", then asserts that nothing was committed. Both offsets are in fact completed by the worker's `finally` (`queue_consumer.py:149`) and would be committed on the next one-second tick. The assertion holds only because the test checks about 0.2s after processing; on a slow run it fails. It should wait for the commit and assert offset 102.

findings.title: New tests are racy or do not assert what their names claim
findings.description:
- **`test_stats_reporting`:** asserts `total_items > 0` right after enqueueing trivial work to live workers, which can already be drained.
- **`test_different_groups_distributed` (lines 98-106):** depends on per-process randomized `hash()` hitting all three queues, so it is probabilistically flaky.
- **`test_preserves_order_within_group` and the "concurrent" tests:** in `TestSimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` they assert only counts, not order or concurrency.
- **`test_thread_queue_parallel_graceful_shutdown`:** asserts only that `queue_pool is None`.
- **Uptime tests:** they poll `qsize() == 0` with sleeps as a completion signal, and never close the strategy, leaking a commit thread per test.
- **Kafka test (`ProcessResultThreadQueueParallelKafkaTest`):** guards its main assertion with `if commits_made:` and swallows cleanup errors with `except Exception: pass`.
- **Missing coverage:** nothing covers rebalance (a second `create_with_partitions`), enqueue failure, or commit-function failure.

findings.title: Docstrings overstate guarantees
findings.description:
- "Only commits offsets after successful processing" is false: the worker completes the offset in `finally` whether or not processing succeeded.
- "Consistent hashing" (`queue_consumer.py:200`) is plain `hash() % n`; that is stable within a process, which is all that is needed, but the term is wrong.
- The `--mode` help text still says "Parallel uses multithreading" without describing the new mode (`src/sentry/consumers/__init__.py:123`).

findings.title: Minor observability and consistency nits
findings.description:
- The worker opens a `sentry_sdk` transaction around `result_processor`, which opens its own (`result_consumer.py:48`), so transactions are nested; the name also embeds the worker id under a `monitors.` prefix.
- The `queue_depth` gauge is emitted by every worker with only the `identifier` tag, so workers overwrite each other.
- The `except queue.ShutDown` around the processor call (`queue_consumer.py:142`) is effectively dead.
- `wait_until_empty` is unused.
- The default of 20 is duplicated at `queue_consumer.py:175` and `result_consumer.py:136`, where `max_workers or 20` also maps 0 to 20.
- The `workers` metric tag is not set for the new mode.

findings.title: Python version compatibility and mode wiring
findings.description: `queue.ShutDown` and `Queue.shutdown` need Python 3.13, which the project requires (`setup.cfg:24`). The CLI choice, the `Literal` type and the dispatch in `create_with_partitions` are consistent. Moving `result_processor` construction earlier in `__init__` is safe, and the `+ 1` on committed offsets is correct.
